teaser: He never fought and never lost a hand. So why paint himself with a stump?
review_notes:
Kirchner enlisted 1915 as an 'involuntary volunteer', trained as a driver with Field Artillery Regiment 75 in Halle, discharged late 1915 after a breakdown; never saw combat.
Painting was in the Städtische Galerie, Frankfurt, confiscated 1937, shown in the Degenerate Art exhibition under the title 'Soldier with Whore'; 639 Kirchner works removed from German museums.
Oberlin acquired it in 1950.
Size about 69 x 61 cm.
Veronal/morphine dependence, sanatorium stays 1915-17, move to Davos 1917, suicide June 1938.

lesson.text: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner made a very bad soldier. Called up in the spring of 1915, he was sent to the town of Halle to train as a driver in an artillery regiment. He could not bear the drill, the horses, the shouting. Within months he had collapsed, and by the end of the year the army let him go.

He never reached the front. He never heard a shot fired in battle. And yet, back in his Berlin studio that same year, he painted himself as a casualty. Everything on this canvas is about a wound that did not happen.
Kirchner called himself an “involuntary volunteer.” He signed up before he could be drafted, hoping that a volunteer would be allowed to choose a safer branch of the army than the infantry.

The picture is small, about 69 by 61 cm (27 by 24 inches), and it is packed tight. Kirchner pushes his own body so close to the edge that the cap is cut off at the top. Start with what the uniform tells you, then go where the eye does not want to go.

lesson.title: Reading the body
lesson.text: Four stops, from the top of the cap down to the raised arm.

spots.title: Eyes without pupils
spots.text: Two flat blue-black patches. No pupil, no glint. He cannot look at his model, at his canvas or at you. For a painter, it is a portrait of blindness.

spots.title: The cigarette
spots.text: It hangs from the corner of a red mouth in a yellow, hollow face. The casual pose of the off-duty soldier, worn by a man who looks ill.

spots.title: Number 75
spots.text: The red shoulder straps carry the number of his real unit, Field Artillery Regiment 75. The uniform is accurate. Only the injury is made up.

spots.title: The stump
spots.text: His right arm ends in a raw cut, green and red like sliced fruit. Kirchner's hand was whole. He painted the thing he feared: a painter who can no longer paint.

lesson.text: A missing painting hand. For Kirchner this was worse than death, and he shows it to you the way a soldier might show a medal. The stump is raised, almost offered. The fear is real even though the amputation is not.
This is a self-portrait of a fear, not of a fact. Expressionism, the movement Kirchner helped start, allowed a painter to show what was true inside even when it was false outside.
Now the rest of the room. He is in his studio, the place where he should be most himself, and the things of his trade stand right behind his back.
Kirchner has turned his back on his work. Can you find the canvas he has left on the easel?

spots.title: The abandoned canvas
spots.text: A streaked pink and red picture leans at the left edge, behind his shoulder. Next to it stands a nude model he does not look at either. Art and desire are both in the room, and both out of reach.

lesson.text: The model is drawn with the same sharp angles as his own face, in the same yellow. Her eyes are closed. Nobody in this painting sees anybody. The warm orange wall and the cold blue uniform press against each other with no air between them.

In the two years after his discharge, Kirchner moved between sanatoriums, dependent on sleeping drugs and morphine. In 1917 he left for Davos in the Swiss Alps, and he stayed in those mountains for the rest of his life.

The painting had a second ordeal. A German museum in Frankfurt owned it until 1937, when the Nazis stripped modern art from public collections. They hung it in their mocking “Degenerate Art” exhibition, an official show meant to make the public laugh at modern painters, under an invented title: “Soldier with Whore.”
More than 600 of Kirchner's works were removed from German museums in 1937. He shot himself near Davos the following year.

The canvas crossed the Atlantic and in 1950 entered a college museum in Oberlin, Ohio, where students now walk past it on their way to class. Go back to those blank blue eyes one more time. A man who failed at being a soldier made one of the most honest pictures of what the war did to people who were never hit.

quiz.question: What really happened to Kirchner's right hand in the war?
options: It was amputated at the front
quiz.explanation: He never reached the front, and his hand was whole.

quiz.question: What does the number 75 on the shoulder straps refer to?
quiz.explanation: He trained with Field Artillery Regiment 75 in Halle.

quiz.question: How are the eyes painted?
options: As flat dark patches with no pupils
quiz.explanation: The empty eyes make a portrait of blindness.

quiz.question: What did the Nazis do with the painting in 1937?
options: They bought it for Hitler's collection
They hung it in the “Degenerate Art” show under a mocking title
quiz.explanation: It was shown as “Soldier with Whore” to ridicule modern art.

facts.text: Kirchner painted this picture in a field hospital near the front line.
facts.explanation: He never reached the front; the scene is set in his studio.

facts.text: Kirchner volunteered so that he might choose a safer branch of the army.
The nude model in the background looks straight at the painter.
facts.explanation: Her eyes are closed; nobody in the picture sees anybody.
